title: The Spectroscopic Atlas of Excitonic Complexes in hBN-Encapsulated S-TMD Monolayers: From Excitons to Oxcitons and Beyond
abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) encapsulation has transformed the optical spectroscopy of semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers (MLs) by suppressing extrinsic disorder and enabling the resolution of an increasingly complex hierarchy of excitonic states. This Review provides a spectroscopy-oriented framework for understanding and identifying excitonic complexes in hBN-encapsulated Mo- and W-based MLs and their alloys. The discussion covers bright and dark excitons, Rydberg states, charged excitons, biexcitons, phonon-assisted replicas, and higher-order Fermi-sea many-body states, including hexcitons and oxcitons, with an emphasis on the experimental signatures that distinguish them. Particular attention is given to the combined use of photoluminescence and absorption-related spectroscopy, electrostatic gating, polarization analysis, excitation-power and temperature dependences, magnetic fields, and time-resolved measurements to establish microscopic assignments. The role of alloying as an additional degree of freedom for engineering the excitonic hierarchy, spin-valley configuration, and magneto-optical response is also highlighted. By organizing the rapidly expanding phenomenology around experimentally accessible fingerprints rather than individual material systems, this Review aims to provide a practical and broadly applicable guide for identifying, comparing, and engineering excitonic states in high-quality two-dimensional semiconductors.
summary: This review provides a comprehensive, spectroscopy-based guide to characterizing the complex hierarchy of excitonic complexes in hBN-encapsulated TMD monolayers. It emphasizes that reliable identification requires combining multiple experimental measurements—such as PL, absorption, and external field tuning—rather than just measuring transition energies. This framework is crucial for engineering and understanding quantum phenomena in 2D semiconductors.
main_problem: To establish a spectroscopy-oriented framework for understanding and identifying the complex hierarchy of excitonic complexes in hBN-encapsulated S-TMD monolayers.
main_result: The identification of these complex excitonic states requires combining multiple experimental observables (e.g., PL, absorption, gating, magnetic fields) rather than relying on transition energy alone.
method: The review synthesizes knowledge from various spectroscopic techniques, including photoluminescence, absorption spectroscopy, and external field/temperature dependence measurements.
model_or_system: The system is semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenide (S-TMD) monolayers (e.g., MoS2, WS2) encapsulated by hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The physics involves a rich hierarchy of many-body excitonic states (excitons, oxcitons, charged excitons) governed by strong Coulomb interactions.
key_observables: Bright/dark exciton energies, A-B exciton separation ($\Delta_{AB}$), Rydberg series spacing, and spectral response to external fields.
important_parameters: Low temperatures, electrostatic gating voltages, magnetic field strengths, and alloying compositions.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the optical response can be systematically organized around experimentally accessible spectroscopic fingerprints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the electronic structure, optical selection rules in the hexagonal Brillouin zone (K± valleys), and the energy splittings between different exciton types (A and B excitons).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical system and the role of hBN encapsulation, then detailing the various types of excitonic complexes, and finally presenting a comprehensive guide based on combined experimental diagnostics.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of excitonic complexes, Rydberg states, and many-body physics in 2D materials provides a rich platform for studying strongly correlated electron physics and open quantum systems dynamics.
